children: By Karishma Vanjani
The global government-bond selloff continued Thursday, even as U.S. Treasury yields eased from multidecade highs.

The rout has gripped long-term debt across the developed world. In the U.S., 10- and 30-year Treasury yields have pulled back slightly from Wednesday's levels, though both briefly touched highs not seen since 2002 Thursday morning.

The carnage in Europe is more pronounced. The French 30-year bond yield settled at 5.5459%, its highest settle since May 27, 2002, while its U.K. 30-year peer settled at 5.93%, just a few basis point shy of its 1993 high.

Higher yields reduce the market value of existing lower-yielding bonds. A 30-year Treasury bond issued on May 15, 2020, with a fixed 1.25% interest rate recently changed hands around a record low price of $426.37, a steep discount from its $1,000 face value, Fidelity brokerage data show. The hit is a direct result of the 30-year yield jumping by almost 4.4 percentage points since the pandemic.

An Austrian 100-year bond-a rare century bond-has lost about 70% of its value since it was issued in 2020. Longer the duration, the bigger the hit from rising yields; for every year of modified duration, a one-percentage-point rise in yields cuts a bond's price by roughly 1%.
"The rise in government bond yields is a structural long-term development," wrote Steven Barrow at Standard Bank on Thursday.

Government bonds rely heavily on a nation's collective pool of savings channeled through corporate pension plans, 401(k)s and other vehicles. But the "strength of equity gains has pushed savings toward stocks and away from bonds" while older people, who generally save less, have grown in number and continue to spend down their savings, he added.

The resumption of a globally synchronized rate-hiking cycle has delivered another impulse for higher yields. The Federal Reserve, the world's most important central bank, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan all delivered a interest-rate hike in the third quarter.
Higher interest rates can push up yields. The 10-year Treasury yield reflects the expectations for future interest rates, among other factors.

"For markets, one of the biggest stories throughout [the third quarter] was the US-Iran conflict, and what that meant for oil prices and inflation," wrote Deutsche Bank's macro strategist Henry Allen. "This backdrop meant central banks shifted in a hawkish direction."

There's also the issue of geopolitical risk, which has made some investors more reluctant to hold U.S. government debt. Congressional estimates put the cost of the armed conflict with Iran at approximately $38 billion as of Aug. 1. Bond investors can demand a higher risk premium when they expect more government spending.

Investors aren't the only casualties of higher global yields. Governments themselves have to pay higher rates to attract buyers during auctions. And when more cash is allocated to interest payments, it leaves less money for roads, bridges, and social programs.
The Treasury Department will auction 10- and 30-year bonds on Oct. 7 and 8, respectively. If demand is weak, yields can go even higher.

Of course, there are idiosyncratic factors, too. In France, the debt burden is set to top 120% of gross domestic product next year. In the U.S., debt held by the public relative to GDP is 99%, but the gross debt to GDP, which includes government obligations to itself, is at 122%. The French government has unveiled plans to restrain spending and raise tax revenue.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent teased a "fiscal consolidation" plan during a CNBC interview on Aug. 20 and in testimony before lawmakers soon after. But one has yet to arrive, and the market needs to believe in its efficacy.
"We remain on the lookout for signs of trend exhaustion, but continue to see little in the price action that favors fading the move," said Jay Barry, J.P. Morgan's head of global rates strategy.
In plain English, he's watching for the selloff to lose momentum but sees little evidence that it is time to bet on a rebound in government bonds.
"We see the rise in yields as a process of financial markets finding their way to this 'new normal' place."
